newsitem.title: UK: France, Germany plan single Euro tax system - paper.
newsitem.headline: France, Germany plan single Euro tax system - paper.

text.p: Plans to create a single European tax system are being privately prepared in Brussels by a powerful alliance of countries including France and Germany, Britain's Independent newspaper said on Thursday.
The proposals envisage control over income tax being pooled by national governments inside the area covered by a planned single European currency, the paper said.
Britain said it was not aware of talks along these lines involving France and Germany.
"We are not aware of any discussions of this sort involving France and Germany," said a spokesman at the office of Prime Minister John Major.
He said Britain did not see the need for such a course of action which would in any case, under EU rules, have to be decided unanimously by all 15 members.

The tax plans, which the paper said were unlikely to have been submitted to the British government, were part of a strategy for a new, "flexible" Europe, the paper said in what it called an exclusive report.
"In practice, they are likely to kill off any chance of Britain joining the single currency in the foreseeable future," the Independent said.

It said the plans would be widely viewed in Britain as an attempt by France and Germany to alter the fundamental character of the European Union radically. It did not say which other EU countries were involved in the planned measures.
British anti-European "Eurosceptics" would now have new cause to argue that Britain's entire relationship with the EU should be renegotiated, the newspaper said.
Opponents of the single currency have always suggested that it would eventually mean a single European economic policy, covering tax and social security.
"The new proposals reveal that Paris and now Bonn agree and are seriously contemplating forging ahead with what will be, in effect, a single hard core economy.

"This thinking is so far ahead of what Westminster (Britain) has contemplated that it makes British membership of EMU (European Economic and Monetary Union), under a Conservative or a Labour government, very unlikely," the Independent said.

The ruling Conservatives are sticking to a "wait and see" approach to whether to join the single European currency in 1999, while the Labour Party, favourite to win an election which must be called by May, has also reserved its options.

The Independent said Germany and France were spearheading a drive to ensure that powers to build a common EU economic policy are written into a "flexibility" chapter in the next treaty on EU reform due in June.
Common policies on direct tax and social security may not be possible until a few years after the EMU launch, France and Germany concede.
But they want the right to go ahead to be written into European law now, as further treaty revisions may not be possible for some time, the paper said.
